props.title: Henry: Portrait of a Serial Killer

sections.content: Henry: Portrait of a Serial Killer redefined screen violence with its unflinching docudrama approach. Director John McNaughton strips away Hollywood's sensationalized serial killer tropes, delivering a cold, observational study that feels more like a documentary than fiction. The film's impact comes from Michael Rooker's chillingly detached performance and the matter-of-fact presentation of Henry's murders. Unlike the gothic flourishes of The Silence of the Lambs (1991) or the dark comedy of American Psycho (2000), McNaughton's film refuses to aestheticize or moralize its violence.

sections.content: The film's legacy shaped a new wave of true crime-inspired horror. Monster (2003) borrowed its documentary-like approach for Aileen Wuornos's story, while The Snowtown Murders (2011) echoed its stark portrayal of violence in working-class settings. McNaughton's innovative use of handheld cameras and natural lighting influenced later found footage horror like Man Bites Dog (1992), which similarly blurred lines between observation and complicity.

The MPAA initially gave Henry an X rating, highlighting how its realism proved more disturbing than supernatural horror or slasher films of the era. While Halloween (1978) and Friday the 13th (1980) offered cathartic thrills, Henry's violence feels mundane and therefore more terrifying. The film's influence extends to modern true crime dramas like Zodiac (2007) and The House That Jack Built (2018), which similarly examine killer psychology without glamorization. sections.content: Henry's documentary aesthetics revolutionized true crime filmmaking. Later works like Summer of Sam (1999) and The Boston Strangler (2023) adopted similar verite techniques to capture period authenticity. The film's influence extends beyond horror into serious drama - Blue Caprice (2013) and My Friend Dahmer (2017) follow Henry's lead in examining killers' mundane daily lives rather than just their crimes.
